entries.note: From Greek [[from:papas]], an affectionate word for father like [[same-root:papa]]; once any bishop, it came to mean only the bishop of Rome about a thousand years ago.
The loving, childish word for father, related to [[same-root:pope]] through Greek papas.
From Greek [[from:episkopos]] via Latin episcopus, from skopos, guardian; nobody knows exactly how it reached northern Europe, and early forms had an sc sound like [[same-root:Episcopal]].
Related to [[same-root:bishop]] even though it looks different: bishop is to Episcopal as [[see:priest]] is to [[see:Presbyterian]].
Borrowed from Latin pastor, shepherd. As late as the 14th century it meant a shepherd or herdsman, but it has long also meant a spiritual guide or minister.
Another parental title, from an Aramaic word for father; Latin made a feminine form of it in the sixth century, which gave [[gave:abbess]].
Comes from a sixth-century Latin feminine form of the word behind [[from:abbot]].
Arch- comes from Latin; the Anglo-Saxons earlier said [[see:hēahbiscop]], and a northern variant was [[see:ass bishop]]. It is the top rank, above [[see:bishop]], [[see:priest]] and [[see:deacon]].
What the Anglo-Saxons called an [[see:archbishop]] before they used the Latin-derived arch- form.
A northern dialect form of [[see:archbishop]] in Old English. It is just a variation on arch-, but the hosts find it funny.
From Latin [[from:presbyter]], from Greek words meaning elder; it could mean anyone with a church position, and ranked below a bishop and above a deacon.
Shares its origin with [[same-root:priest]], just as [[see:Episcopal]] does with bishop.
The specific term for the [[see:priest]] who stood at the front of the church and read aloud, as opposed to anyone holding a church position.
From Greek diakonos via Latin, meaning a servant or messenger, which fits its rank below a [[see:priest]].
Related to [[same-root:minimum]], [[same-root:minus]] and [[same-root:minor]]: a humble servant or underling, hence [[see:prime minister]]. It is less related to [[unrelated:minster]] than it looks.
Related to [[same-root:minister]], sharing the idea of something lesser.
Related to [[same-root:minister]], sharing the idea of something lesser.
Related to [[same-root:minister]], sharing the idea of something lesser.
Uses [[see:minister]] in its sense of servant: someone who serves the public good.
A big cathedral, of which only a handful exist. It comes from Greek monos, alone, like [[same-root:monk]], and is less related to [[unrelated:minister]] than it seems.
From Latin [[from:cardinalis]], from a word for a hinge, because cardinals were pivotal to the church; the bird and the colour are named after cardinals' red robes.
Numbers like one, two, three, four, named with [[see:cardinal]] in its sense of pivotal or important.
The cardinals' gathering to choose a pope; from Latin con, with, and clavis, key. It was first the lockable room where they met, then the meeting itself.
From Greek monos, alone, like [[same-root:monastery]] and [[same-root:minster]]; Old English made a feminine form of its predecessor, [[gave:mynecen]].
A place to live alone, from Greek monos, alone, like [[same-root:monk]].
Another parental-figure word, related to [[same-root:nana]]; Old English also had [[see:mynecen]], a female monk.
A word for grandmother, said to be related to [[same-root:nun]].
A feminine form of the Old English predecessor of [[from:monk]], basically a lady monk; it sounds very like the old name of [[see:Munich]].
A city founded by Benedictine monks; its older name, Munichen, essentially means monk town and resembles Old English [[see:mynecen]].
A place to come together, related to [[same-root:convene]].
Shares its origin with [[same-root:convent]], a place to convene.
From the Greek for desert or uninhabited place, so literally a person of the desert. Christianity took it up through stories of wandering the desert for trials.
From French, via Latin clericus, from Greek [[from:klēros]], lot or inheritance, after Deuteronomy's Levites, whose inheritance was the Lord. Clergy were spiritual heirs.
Popular from the 1620s, from Greek klērikos, belonging to the clergy; perhaps an overcorrection after [[same-root:clerk]] went secular.
Shares a root with [[same-root:clergy]]; in the 1200s it meant a priest. It became secular because literate clergy worked as record keepers, accountants and royal scribes.
Anglican church set up by [[see:Henry VIII]] to get a divorce the pope refused. Rob finds it very tame, largely about lemon drizzle cake.
Set up the [[see:Church of England]] because he wanted another divorce and the pope wouldn't allow it.
The denomination of Jess's extended family, which she describes as derived from Anglicanism and very relaxed, mostly about rebuilding houses knocked over by tornadoes.
Referred to the building first; from Greek kyriakon doma, the Lord's house, so going to God's house is quite literal.
From Latin cappella, cape: the original chapel was where the Frankish kings kept the [[from:cape of St. Martin]]. The word later meant any reliquary.
The half cloak that [[see:Saint Martin]] kept, treated as a sacred relic by Frankish kings; the place it was kept was the original [[gave:chapel]].
Literally where the bishop's seat is, meaning his chair or his headquarters. Like a [[see:chapel]], it is named for what it contains, so it needn't be big.
While serving in Rome, he cut his cloak in half to share with a beggar, then dreamed of Christ wearing it; his half became the [[see:cape of St. Martin]].
From [[from:cappellani]], the people who looked after the relic of the [[see:cape of St. Martin]].
A Jewish meeting house, literally a place to meet, from the Greek for to bring together.
A European mangling of Arabic [[from:masjid]], a temple, or more literally a place of prostration.
A Sikh place of worship. It contains [[see:guru]] and dvara, Sanskrit for door, a cognate of [[same-root:door]] that shows English and Sanskrit are related.
The community kitchens at a [[see:gurdwara]], where anyone can get a full meal for free.
What Sikhs call their spiritual leaders, including their book, the [[see:Guru Granth Sahib]]; the word is hidden in [[see:gurdwara]].
The Sikh holy book, regarded as the final [[see:guru]].
Strikingly close to Sanskrit dvara in [[same-root:gurdwara]], a reminder that English and Sanskrit are related.
From Latin regula, rule, like [[same-root:ruler]]. Around 1400 it first meant someone following a monastic rule, then spread to shapes, patterns and behaviour.
Shares with [[same-root:regular]] the Latin root for a rule or straight piece.
Originally ecclesiastically suspect: it described something that broke church rules, the counterpart of [[see:regular]].
Literally above nature; it first referred to divine intervention, miracles and God's unexplainable power, rather than to ghosts.
From Greek enthousiasmos, possessed by a god, containing theos. At first it was negative in English, like calling someone a man possessed.
Means to breathe in; the idea was breathing in some holy essence, like the Greek oracles did.
Literally all demons; first used in [[from:Paradise Lost]] as the name of Satan's palace, the capital city of hell.
John Milton's poem, the source of much religious lore that people assume is biblical, and of [[gave:pandemonium]].
A Hebrew plural of respect meaning great beast, borrowed in [[see:John Wycliffe]]'s Bible. It was read as elephant, then [[see:hippopotamus]], its meaning in Russian and Ukrainian.
His Bible translation took [[see:behemoth]] straight from Hebrew, and he introduced the Latinised [[see:revelation]] in the 1300s.
Used as a word for something large, like [[see:behemoth]], with story lore behind it.
Named after [[from:Gargantua and Pantagruel]]; another word for big things with story lore behind it.
An extremely lewd, far-from-religious story that gave us [[gave:gargantuan]].
Means river horse; the amphibious biblical [[see:behemoth]] came to be identified with it.
From Latin biblia sacra, holy books, a plural taken as singular, via Greek biblion from byblos, papyrus, probably after the port of [[from?:Byblos]].
Shares its origin with [[same-root:Bible]], whose source word biblia meant books.
A Phoenician port in modern Lebanon that exported Egyptian papyrus, probably the ultimate source of [[gave:Bible]], so the Bible is named after a shipping hub.
The French word for library; like [[same-root:Bible]], it is supposedly named after a faraway port.
A word or practice that reveals group membership. In Judges, the [[see:Gileadites]] killed [[see:Ephraimites]] who, lacking a sh sound, said sibboleth.
Means left-handed, as Jess explains in her book, which a negative review called full of sinister shibboleths.
A film where Michael Fassbender's character holds up three fingers the wrong way and is exposed as not a Nazi: a gesture [[see:shibboleth]].
After winning a war against the [[see:Ephraimites]], they blockaded the Jordan and used [[see:shibboleth]] to catch Ephraimites trying to cross.
Their language lacked the sh sound, so they said sibboleth and were killed by the [[see:Gileadites]] at the Jordan.
A Derbyshire village whose pronunciation, close to Jess's guess rhyming with kite, works as a local [[see:shibboleth]]; it has a tramway museum.
From a Latin word for a building; church writers used it for building up the soul like a spiritual house. By the 1600s it meant mental and moral development.
First a weight, usually of silver, then a coin; its sense of a God-given ability comes from the [[from:parable of the talents]].
A Greek [[see:talent]] was worth 6,000 drachmae, and Rob only just learned that drachmae is the plural of drachma.
A parable in Matthew where a master gives three servants talents; two invest theirs and double them, which gave [[gave:talent]] its modern sense.
A TV programme Rob thinks should be called Britain's Been Practising, since contestants show skills rather than [[see:talent]].
The Greek name for the Book of [[see:revelation]], meaning an unveiling, from apo, off, plus cover. Its end-of-the-world sense came recently through [[see:apocalypticism]].
The same idea as [[see:apocalypse]], Latinised by [[see:John Wycliffe]] in the 1300s; its link to [[same-root:reveal]] is hidden by the difference in pronunciation.
Related to [[same-root:revelation]], though the different pronunciations obscure the link.
The belief that the Revelation was near, which gave [[see:apocalypse]] its end-of-the-world sense.
Contains the Greek for hidden, as in [[same-root:cryptocurrency]]. It first meant hidden, then of dubious origin, so an apocryphal tale probably isn't true.
Shares the Greek element for hidden with [[same-root:apocryphal]].
Where God banishes Cain after he kills Abel, east of Eden; [[see:Jonathan Swift]] first used it for sleep, punning on the older [[see:nodding off]].
The location of [[see:the land of Nod]] in the Cain story, and the title of a Steinbeck novel full of Cain and Abel parallels.
Credited as the first to use [[see:the land of Nod]] to mean going to bed, punning on [[see:nodding off]].
Existed long before [[see:the land of Nod]] meant sleep, so Swift's use was a pun on it.
From [[from:Belshazzar]], who saw a disembodied hand write [[see:mene, mene, tekel, upharsin]] on his wall; it foretold his overthrow, and he was dead by morning.
A king who saw a hand writing on his wall, was told he would be overthrown, and was dead by morning: the origin of [[gave:the writing on the wall]].
The creepy inscription at [[see:Belshazzar]]'s feast foretelling his overthrow; mene mene is sometimes said instead of [[equivalent:the writing on the wall]], almost a shibboleth.
